# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](AGENTS.md#prose-form). It contains near term tasks with a short
description and uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the problem overview and its list of
things to do. That is followed by the "plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

_No cycle currently in progress._

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank**, #1 highest, descending. Reprioritize by moving an
entry, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber. The numbers are positional rank,
not stable IDs. To refer to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention; a numbered
list item has no anchor to link to), not its number. Long-tail entries live in
[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper detail goes in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Power policy is this box's dominant reproducibility factor: record it, gate on it, and fix
   LSC's scope (measured 2026-08-03; the session's terminal stamps read 26-08-04 UTC)
   - the measurement: `min-now --blocks 200`, 8 pinned + 8 unpinned per policy, alternating so
     box history is shared between conditions, under amd-pstate-epp `powersave` then
     `performance`
     - powersave unpinned: 23.927 ns, run-to-run stdev 0.785 ns (3.28%), grades 4 A / 2 D / 2 F
     - powersave pinned to one core: 22.207 ns, 0.073 ns (0.33%), all 8 graded D
     - performance unpinned: 21.980 ns, 0.057 ns (0.26%), no D or F in 17 runs
     - performance pinned: 22.359 ns, 0.311 ns (1.39%)
     - so EPP moves the number 8% and run-to-run scatter 12x, and it inverts the pinning
       answer: pinning wins under powersave and loses under performance
   - the finding that reframes the grade: A was being awarded to the un-boosted floor. A
     powersave A run puts ~73% of its samples on 23.967 ns, the 3.7929 GHz TSC/base rate, while
     the boosted states are 21.79 / 22.22. Flatness is all the grade sees, and base clock is
     the flattest place on the box
   - do first, cheap: print driver / governor / EPP / boost in `Setup:`; the sysfs reader
     already exists in `src/freq.rs`
     - no report in the project's history records the policy, so every archived number is
       ambiguous
     - an A/B spanning a policy change reads a 9% delta as code
   - then: `qualify-environment` reads the policy as a fitness precondition and says so before
     spending minutes on numbers it can predict will scatter
     - a diagnosis, never a mutation: setting the governor needs root and is global and
       persistent, and this session's documented revert left EPP at `performance` after the
       governor had already returned to `powersave`
   - bug, wants its own bugs.md entry: LSC is scoped to within-run block agreement but reads as
     a run-to-run bound
     - the best configuration printed LSC 0.022 ns against a measured run-to-run stdev of
       0.057 ns, so single-run against single-run resolution is ~0.157 ns (0.71%) where the
       report prints 0.10%
     - about 7x optimistic, and it did not improve when the environment did
     - the fix wants a run-to-run component; `qualify-environment` already spawns the repeated
       children that would measure it
   - evidence is perishable: `tmp/pinexp/` holds only the performance series (the rerun
     overwrote powersave), so the powersave numbers live only in the session transcript until
     copied into a chores design subsection
   - cross-cuts the entries below: the interpretation guide's worked trio and the blocks entry's
     duty-cycle evidence were both collected without recording the policy, and a four-run
     `--blocks` sweep this session proved confounded (block count and box history rose
     together, history dominating), so re-check those examples before they ship as teaching
     material
   - raises "Seam-clock attribution" (below): we think today's three states map onto ~3.79 /
     4.17 / 4.35 GHz, inferred from timing ratios alone, and a seam clock sample would settle it
2. Report interpretation guide: a reader-oriented "how to read a report" walkthrough in README,
   teaching what each surface means and, above all, what to conclude from it
   - surfaces to cover:
     - the band table: first/last/range/count/mean per quantile band
     - the summary rows: mean/stdev, the trimmed row, blocks mean/CI95/LSC
     - the grade block: env warmup/bench vs run rows, per-signal letters, the settle cell
     - the -v warmup table and its exit/window/clock summary line
   - lead with worked examples, the 2026-08-02 3900X trio (plain -d 5, --blocks 100,
     --blocks 1000):
     - duty cycle selects the bistable state: sustained load climbs into the fast state
       (~21.8 ns), while 5 ms bursts between 1-10 ms sleeps hold the slow state (24.0 ns)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Alternating pinned/unpinned repeatability series at --blocks 200.
# History is the known confound, so conditions alternate and the first run is discarded.
set -u
D=tmp/pinexp
iiac-perf min-now --decimals 3 --blocks 200 > "$D/prime.txt" 2>&1
for i in $(seq 1 8); do
  iiac-perf min-now --decimals 3 --blocks 200            > "$D/u$i.txt" 2>&1
  iiac-perf min-now --decimals 3 --blocks 200 --pin 4    > "$D/p$i.txt" 2>&1
done
echo done

content.text:
Read TODO #1, the surviving series in `tmp/pinexp/`, and the CLI surface. Thoughts below, no changes made.

## What the evidence actually supports

The performance half is fully checkable, and it reproduces the TODO's numbers exactly. From the 17
files in `tmp/pinexp/` (`mean blocks` per run):

- unpinned n=8: mean 21.980, stdev 0.0567 (0.26%)
- pinned n=8: mean 22.359, stdev 0.311 (1.39%)
- no D or F in any of the 17 `run all` grades

So the performance-side arithmetic in TODO #1 is sound. Two things it does not say, though:

- **The pinned series is bimodal, not scattered.** p1,p2,p7,p8 sit at 22.08-22.09; p3,p4,p5,p6 sit
  at 22.59-22.70. That is not run-to-run noise around a mean, it is four consecutive runs in a
  different state. The 0.311 ns stdev is a summary of a state change, and quoting it as "pinning's
  scatter" reads it as the wrong kind of quantity. The unpinned runs interleaved with those four
  did not move, which is interesting on its own and unexplained.
- **The powersave half is not on disk.** TODO #1 already flags this ("the rerun overwrote
  powersave"), but the consequence is worth stating plainly: the 8% and the 12x both depend on
  numbers that now exist only in a session transcript, and I cannot re-derive either.

## Where the claim overreaches

The sentence bundles three assertions of very different strength.

- "EPP moves the number 8%": 23.927 vs 21.980 is 8.9%, and it is a between-block comparison. The
  two policies were not alternated (they cannot be cheaply: flipping EPP needs root and is global
  and persistent), so time and box history are confounded with policy. That is precisely the
  confound TODO #1 itself uses to invalidate the `--blocks` sweep two bullets later. The effect is
  large enough that I would still expect it to survive, but the current experiment does not
  separate the two.
- "run-to-run scatter 12x": that ratio is 3.28% / 0.26%, the relative figures, not the 0.785 /
  0.057 absolute ratio (13.8x). Fine, but the reader cannot tell which is meant.
- "it inverts the pinning answer": the two halves of the inversion are not equally supported. Under
  powersave, pinned beat unpinned by 7% with an order-of-magnitude scatter reduction, which is a
  big, hard-to-fake effect. Under performance, pinned "lost" by 1.7%, and that entire loss comes
  from the four-run cluster above. Drop those four and pinning is a wash. Calling that an inversion
  is the weakest link in the sentence, and it is the part the TODO leans on hardest.

My read: the powersave-vs-performance delta is probably real and probably large. The inversion is a
single-experiment artifact until shown otherwise. The TODO should be re-worded to that effect
whether or not we rerun.

## On rerunning, and on building the capability

Checked history: nothing like this was ever in the tool and removed. Deletions in `src/` are
`overhead.rs`, the zcr raw/spin tiers, `tsc.rs`, and `timer.rs`. So this is new capability, not a
restoration. The nearest existing machinery is `qualify-environment`, which already spawns N child
runs and tabulates them, plus `--pin` and the sysfs reader in `freq.rs`.

I would sequence it as three separable pieces, smallest first, and I would not rerun before the
first two land:

1. **Stamp the policy in `Setup:`.** Already TODO #1's "do first, cheap". Without it a rerun
   produces exactly the same ambiguous artifacts we are complaining about. This is the gate.
2. **Make a run's result machine-readable and durable.** The reason this evidence perished is that
   the only record was formatted text in a scratch dir, and the only extraction path was `grep` for
   `mean blocks`. A per-run record (one JSON object: policy stamp, pin spec, mean/stdev/CI95/LSC,
   the grade letters, timestamp, run index) written to a file makes any future series re-analyzable
   without the transcript. This is the highest value-per-line item on the list and it is useful
   even if the series harness never gets built.
3. **A series/compare subcommand.** Runs a condition matrix with alternation and a discarded prime
   run, and reports per-condition run-to-run mean and stdev, which is the number the tool currently
   never prints. Design points I think matter:
   - It must report the per-run sequence, not just mean and stdev, or it will summarize the next
     bimodal cluster into a scatter figure the same way this one did.
   - It must refuse to pool runs whose policy stamps differ, and instead report them as separate
     blocks with the confound named.
   - It cannot set EPP, and should not try: root, global, persistent, and this session's own revert
     already left the box in a mixed state. The honest shape is either "record and join two
     operator-run series" or an interactive mode that pauses and asks the operator to flip the
     policy between blocks, which is the only way to interleave policy in time.
   - More reps than 8, given what 8 just produced.

The bonus is that this is the same machinery TODO #1's LSC bug needs: LSC's problem is that it
bounds within-run block agreement while reading as a run-to-run bound, and a run-to-run component
requires exactly the repeated-child series above. One capability serves the policy stamp, the
rerun, and the LSC fix.

**The plain version:** the performance numbers check out against the files, but the powersave ones
only exist in a transcript, and the "pinning loses under performance" half rests on four runs that
drifted together. Worth rerunning, but only after the tool stamps the power policy and writes
machine-readable per-run records, otherwise the rerun perishes the same way. The series harness is
the third step, and it should never touch EPP itself.

1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
9	[custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## File reads: read the slice you need
12	
13	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs; grep or read
14	further on demand.
15	
16	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
17	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
18	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read further only when chasing a
19	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
20	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
21	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it first.
22	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small; read whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
23	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
24	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
25	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
26	  need.
27	
28	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
29	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule applies
30	to historical files.
31	
32	## Notes references
33	
34	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
35	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
36	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
37	single-bracketed.
38	
39	## Reference numbering
40	
41	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
42	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
43	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
44	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
45	
46	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
47	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
48	file's number; to cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
49	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
50	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
51	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no definition here. To
52	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
53	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
54	
55	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
56	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
57	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
58	as-built ladder. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
59	exact shape.
60	
61	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
62	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
63	then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
64	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
65	definitions move; every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
66	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
67	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
68	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
69	append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
70	slots out of document order).
71	
72	## Markdown anchor links
73	
74	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
75	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
76	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
77	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
78	official spec for auto-generated anchors; the de-facto reference implementation is
79	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
80	
81	## Todo format
82	
83	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
84	long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
85	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
86	description with reference links to more detail.
87	
88	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
89	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
90	an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
91	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
92	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
93	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
94	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
95	
96	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
97	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
98	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
99	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
100	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
101	
102	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
103	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
104	
105	Example shape:
106	
107	```
108	# Todo
109	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
110	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
111	
112	# Done
113	- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]
114	
115	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
116	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
117	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
118	```
119	
120	## Retiring Done entries
121	
122	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
123	log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:
124	
125	- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
126	  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
127	- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
128	  version-of-record.
129	
130	Migration mechanics:
131	
132	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
133	  number).
134	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
135	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
136	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
137	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
138	
139	## Chores conventions
140	
141	### Headings and entries that record a commit
142	
143	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
144	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
145	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
146	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
147	`(<version>)` suffix**; see
148	[Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
149	header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
150	`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
151	title.
152	
153	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
154	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
155	whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
156	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.
157	
158	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
159	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
160	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
161	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
162	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
163	
164	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
165	free-form text; the convention applies going forward.
166	
167	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
168	
169	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
170	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
171	design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
172	per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
173	"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
174	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
175	restates the other.
176	
177	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
178	ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
179	*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
180	cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
181	the pointer, so the two don't drift.
182	
183	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
184	promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
185	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
186	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
187	direction).
188	
189	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
190	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
191	narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
192	
193	### Chores commit references
194	
195	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
196	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
197	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
198	one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:
199	
200	```
201	## refactor: extract config loader
202	
203	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
204	- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader
205	
206	<intro paragraph...>
207	```
208	
209	- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
210	  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
211	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
212	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
213	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
214	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
215	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
216	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
217	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
218	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
219	
220	```
221	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
222	```
223	
224	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
225	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
226	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
227	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
228	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
229	
230	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
231	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
232	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
233	`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
234	permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
235	record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
236	[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
237	
238	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
239	going forward.
240	
241	### Chores file Table of Contents
242	
243	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
244	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
245	section, in file order.
246	
247	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
248	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
249	- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
250	  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
251	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
252	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.
253

source of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
before editing a notes file.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## File reads: read the slice you need

Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs; grep or read
further on demand.

- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with

- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small; read whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
  need.

**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule applies
to historical files.

## Notes references

Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
single-bracketed.

## Reference numbering

Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.

Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
file's number; to cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no definition here. To
point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.

A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
as-built ladder. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
exact shape.

A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
definitions move; every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
slots out of document order).

## Markdown anchor links

GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
official spec for auto-generated anchors; the de-facto reference implementation is
[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).

## Todo format

`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
description with reference links to more detail.

`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.

Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.

`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.

Example shape:

```
# Todo
1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
2. Fix bug Y [[1]]

# Done
- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
[2]: issues.md#issue-z
[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
```

## Retiring Done entries

`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
  version-of-record.

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
`(<version>)` suffix**; see
[Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
title.

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text; the convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
restates the other.

The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
the pointer, so the two don't drift.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
8	[custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## Prose form
11	
12	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
13	or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet list for the details. Wrap lines at <=100 cols,
14	commit titles and bodies at <=72 (bullet continuations indent two spaces); existing text
15	re-wraps when touched, no mass sweeps. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure
16	that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is
17	the same failure at sentence scale; see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets)
18	and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
19	
20	Surfaces that use this shape:
21	
22	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
23	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
24	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
25	  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
26	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
27	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
28	- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure
29	  one-liners are still fine.
30	
31	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
32	
33	- **Commit bodies**: bullets are file-by-file, one bullet per file changed, file plus a
34	  one-line gist (e.g. `README.md: new Overview intro`), detail as sub-bullets in short sentence
35	  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Source of truth for the mechanical edit list.
36	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
37	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
38	  list; see
39	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
40	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
41	
42	### Problem + plan shape
43	
44	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo` entries use a sharper form
45	of the same shape:
46	
47	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences; don't pad with intent, don't restate
48	  the plan.
49	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when): formality differs by surface:
50	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit; see
51	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
52	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
53	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering; formalized only when the entry is
54	    picked up into a cycle.
55	
56	### Semicolons inside bullets
57	
58	A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`) is a list hiding inside
59	running prose: break the clauses into sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running
60	prose (intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very short clauses or tight
61	pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when breaking would be more noise than signal.
62	
63	### Typeable punctuation only
64	
65	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`.
66	None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
67	dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is
68	absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
69	them.
70	
71	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
72	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
73	
74	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
75	  sub-bullets.
76	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
77	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
78	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
79	  go.
80	
81	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
82	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
83	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
84	commit.
85	
86	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
87	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
88	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
89	prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
90	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
91	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
92	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
93	
94	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
95	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
96	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
97	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
98	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
99	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
100	
101	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
102	
103	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
104	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
105	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
106	They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
107	file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
108	shared template:
109	
110	```
111	<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
112	<optional prose intro>
113	  - <optional item>
114	    <optional prose intro>
115	      - <optional sub-item>
116	      ...
117	```
118	
119	The three surfaces apply it as:
120	
121	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
122	  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
123	  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
124	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
125	  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
126	  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
127	- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
128	  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
129	  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).
130	
131	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
132	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
133	reuse it.
134	
135	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
136	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
137	section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
138	with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
139	
140	## Speculation marker
141	
142	Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
143	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
144	hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
145	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
146	
147	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
148	session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
149	worth keeping visible in the written record.
150	
151	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
152	"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
153	("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
154	prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
155	on hand.
156	
157	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
158	
159	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
160	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
161	the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.
162	
163	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
164	misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.
165	
166	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
167	the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
168	synopsis.

  go.

Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
commit.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
shared template:

```
<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The three surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).

The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
worth keeping visible in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
on hand.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
synopsis.

1	# jj and cross-repo linking
2	
3	How version control is driven on this project (jj, never raw git) and how the two repos'
4	commits point at each other (the `ochid:` trailer). Read this before any jj operation beyond
5	`st` / `log` / `diff`, and always before touching a commit description.
6	
7	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
8	[custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## jj Basics
11	
12	**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log, diff, commit, push, history
13	rewrite). jj coexists with the git backend, so the repo *can* be driven with raw `git`, but
14	this project's workflow (bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid trailers) is expressed in
15	jj terms; reaching for `git` invites state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There
16	is no `jj mv`: to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and jj detects the rename by
17	content.
18	
19	- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude`: show working copy status
20	- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude`: show commit log
21	- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: finalize working copy into a commit
22	- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: set description without committing
23	- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>`: push a bookmark (no `--allow-new` flag; jj pushes
24	  new bookmarks without special flags)
25	- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited. `jj commit` finalizes it
26	  and creates a new empty working copy on top.
27	- The bot repo always has uncommitted changes during an active session because session data
28	  updates continuously.
29	- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).
30	
31	## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)
32	
33	The cross-reference between the work repo and the bot repo is what makes the dual-repo work:
34	every commit points at its counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the
35	"why / how" (session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the **ochid** (Other Change ID)
36	git trailer.
37	
38	A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s
39	(unlike the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the
40	counterpart commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:
41	
42	- Paths start with `/`, the workspace root, i.e. the work repo (the project root). `/.claude`
43	  is the bot sub-repo.
44	- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work repo**.
45	- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **bot repo**.
46	
47	Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the
48	chid's **12-character** prefix:
49	
50	```
51	ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to a bot-repo change
52	ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
53	```
54	
55	How many, and which direction:
56	
57	- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>`, the bot repo's change ID.
58	- **The bot-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push.
59	  The count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as
60	  they landed still carries exactly one; more than one occurs when a single push publishes
61	  several work-repo commits.
62	
63	Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,bot -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work repo, second bot
64	repo).
65	
66	`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**; never hand-write them into a commit body or
67	`--title`/`--body`.
68	
69	## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer
70	
71	**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
72	coordinating with everyone involved first.** It is a history rewrite, and it silently drops the
73	cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been described and carries no
74	trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not covered; that is the
75	sub-cycle ladder's
76	[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
77	step 4.
78	
79	When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
80	hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one
81	already stamped). Hit at the 0.77.2 amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that
82	way; `vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.
83	
84	## Resolvability
85	
86	A change ID travels with its commit: a **pushed** commit resolves to the same chid in every
87	clone; cloning the bot repo gave the published `main` tip the same chid as an existing clone.
88	We think jj carries the change ID in the git commit object, so it survives `jj git clone` /
89	fetch.
90	
91	The local-only case is the **working-copy `@`**: jj mints a fresh random chid for `@` in each
92	clone, so an unpushed `@` is never a stable ochid target. This is why a bot-repo ochid names
93	`@-` (the last committed change), not `@`.
94	
95	## .vc-config.toml
96	
97	Each repo contains a `.vc-config.toml` whose `[repos]` registry records the workspace layout.
98	Values are ordinary paths relative to the config file's directory (absolute allowed,
99	discouraged), so the two sides' blocks **differ**: the entry that resolves to the config's own
100	directory names its side, and the two sides must agree on the same resolved work/bot pair:
101	
102	```toml
103	# work side          # bot side
104	[repos]              [repos]
105	work = "."           work = ".."
106	bot = ".claude"      bot = "."
107	```
108	
109	Ochid trailer prefixes are fixed per-side labels (`/` work, `/.claude` bot) resolved by side
110	detection, not filesystem paths.

git trailer.

A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s
(unlike the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the
counterpart commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:

- Paths start with `/`, the workspace root, i.e. the work repo (the project root). `/.claude`
  is the bot sub-repo.
- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work repo**.
- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **bot repo**.

Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the
chid's **12-character** prefix:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to a bot-repo change
ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
```

How many, and which direction:

- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>`, the bot repo's change ID.
- **The bot-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push.
  The count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as
  they landed still carries exactly one; more than one occurs when a single push publishes
  several work-repo commits.

Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,bot -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work repo, second bot
repo).

`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**; never hand-write them into a commit body or
`--title`/`--body`.

## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer

**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
coordinating with everyone involved first.** It is a history rewrite, and it silently drops the
cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been described and carries no
trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not covered; that is the
sub-cycle ladder's
[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
step 4.

When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one
already stamped). Hit at the 0.77.2 amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that
way; `vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.

## Resolvability

A change ID travels with its commit: a **pushed** commit resolves to the same chid in every
clone; cloning the bot repo gave the published `main` tip the same chid as an existing clone.
We think jj carries the change ID in the git commit object, so it survives `jj git clone` /
fetch.

The local-only case is the **working-copy `@`**: jj mints a fresh random chid for `@` in each
clone, so an unpushed `@` is never a stable ochid target. This is why a bot-repo ochid names
`@-` (the last committed change), not `@`.

## .vc-config.toml

Each repo contains a `.vc-config.toml` whose `[repos]` registry records the workspace layout.
Values are ordinary paths relative to the config file's directory (absolute allowed,
discouraged), so the two sides' blocks **differ**: the entry that resolves to the config's own
directory names its side, and the two sides must agree on the same resolved work/bot pair:

```toml
# work side          # bot side
[repos]              [repos]
work = "."           work = ".."
bot = ".claude"      bot = "."
```

Ochid trailer prefixes are fixed per-side labels (`/` work, `/.claude` bot) resolved by side
detection, not filesystem paths.

input.description: Check aarch64 clock and dither module

content.text:
Checked what's already there before answering, since it changes the estimate: `serde` with `derive` is a
dependency but `serde_json` is not, `src/ticks/aarch64.rs` exists so the rpi5 is a supported target,
and `src/freq.rs` reads cpufreq sysfs but only `cpuinfo_avg_freq` / `cpuinfo_max_freq`. The policy
fields (driver, governor, EPP, boost) are new readers, not a wiring job.

## Display plus file, and it is genuinely not much trouble

The trick is to not make it a mode. The human report stays on stdout exactly as it is today, always,
and the record is a side channel:

- `--record <PATH>`: append one JSON object per run, one line per run (NDJSON).
- Display unchanged and unconditional, so "I want to see it too" costs zero design.

NDJSON over a JSON array because a series is then just N invocations pointing at the same file,
which is what `run.sh` already does. Appending needs no reparse, an interrupted series leaves a
valid file, and `jq -s .` gives you an array when you want one. Cost is `serde_json` plus a
`#[derive(Serialize)]` record struct.

## The one addition that makes the reruns work: `--tag k=v`

Recorded verbatim in the record, otherwise ignored. That is what lets the driving script label
`--tag condition=pinned --tag policy=performance --tag box=3900x` without the tool needing to know
what a series is. It means we can rerun the experiment on all three boxes *before* building any
series harness, and the harness later just consumes the same NDJSON.

## What a record has to carry

The rule: enough that no transcript is ever needed again. Concretely:

- **host**: hostname, arch, CPU model, logical CPU count, kernel version
- **policy**: `scaling_driver`, `scaling_governor`, `energy_performance_preference`, `boost`, each
  an `Option` recorded as absent rather than defaulted, plus whether they are uniform across CPUs
- **clock**: ticks/ns and its source (calibrated TSC vs `CNTFRQ_EL0`)
- **invocation**: version, bench, `-d`, `--blocks`, outer/inner, pin spec, warm settings, argv
- **ordering**: wall-clock start per run. This is what let me spot the p3-p6 cluster; without it a
  series is an unordered bag and that finding is invisible
- **results**: mean, stdev, trimmed pair, blocks mean, CI95, LSC, and the band table rows
- **grades**: both env rows and the run row, per-signal letter and value, settle, and the
  "not settled" / "uncertified" flags

## Three-box caveats worth knowing before we run

- **rpi5-20cd has no EPP.** cpufreq there is governor-only, so its arm of the experiment is
  pinned-vs-unpinned under whatever governors exist. The absent-vs-zero distinction in the record is
  what keeps that honest, and the analysis must not assume an EPP field exists.
- **rpi5's clock lattice is 18.5 ns** (54 MHz Generic Timer) against a ~20 ns measurement.
  `DITHER_SPAN` is sized at ~26-32 ns, i.e. ~3 quanta on a ~10 ns x86 lattice but only ~1.5 there.
  We think the dither still randomizes phase adequately, but it is close enough to one quantum that
  I would rather verify it on the box than assume it. If it does not, the rpi5's quantization error
  is not zero-mean and its numbers are not comparable to the x86 boxes even in shape.
- **`--pin 4` is not portable** across 3900X and 7600x. The script should pick the core by rule, and
  the record carries the resolved spec either way.
- **Only within-box comparisons mean anything.** The output of interest per box is its
  pinned-vs-unpinned delta and its run-to-run scatter, not nanoseconds compared across boxes.

## Effect on the ladder

The record work moves up next to the policy stamp, because the reruns are the point:

- `feat: record the power policy in Setup`
- `feat: write a per-run JSON record` (`--record`, `--tag`, serde_json)
- then the reruns on all three boxes, as evidence captured in a chores design subsection, not a rung
- `feat: qualify-environment gates on the policy`
- `fix: LSC gains a run-to-run component`
- close-out

The series harness drops off this cycle entirely. With `--record` and `--tag` it stops being a
prerequisite and becomes a convenience we can build once we know what the analysis actually wants.

**The plain version:** the report keeps printing to the screen just like now, and we add a flag that
also appends one line of machine-readable data per run to a file you name. A second flag lets the
script label each run ("pinned", "performance", "3900x"), so all three boxes can write into
comparable files and nothing depends on a chat transcript ever again. Two small features get us to
the rerun; the fancier experiment-runner can wait. The one thing I want to check on the Pi before
trusting its numbers is that its much coarser clock does not bias the measurement.

Want me to write the `## In Progress` block and chores section for that ladder?

content.content:
1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md); on any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
9	[custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## The cycle at a glance
12	
13	Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`, optional) -> Work commits
14	(`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare `X.Y.Z`). The version suffix encodes the phase;
15	the scheme, and where the version-of-record lives, are in
16	[versioning.md](../notes/versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md)
17	before any commit work, and before any push, cycle or not.
18	
19	## Committing vs pushing
20	
21	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
22	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
23	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
24	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
25	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
26	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
27	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
28	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
29	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).
30	
31	## Per-commit checklist
32	
33	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
34	[Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
35	
36	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
37	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
38	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
39	4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
40	   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
41	5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
42	   complete.
43	6. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, prose body (work repo: file-by-file,
44	   opening with the version-bump bullet). See
45	   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
46	7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
47	   explicitly includes it.
48	8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
49	   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.
50

# Cycle checklists

Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
[cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md); on any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## The cycle at a glance

Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`, optional) -> Work commits
(`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare `X.Y.Z`). The version suffix encodes the phase;
the scheme, and where the version-of-record lives, are in
[versioning.md](../notes/versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md)
before any commit work, and before any push, cycle or not.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
6. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, prose body (work repo: file-by-file,
   opening with the version-bump bullet). See
   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe; the commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed; the close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval; "commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only; destructive ops still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`), per the protocol's
[Close-out](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. Move the picked-up item from `## In Progress` to a one-line `## Done` entry with its chores
   `[N]` ref.
2. Finalize the chores section: sync the header to the final commit title (and every anchor
   back-reference), add design subsections; the intro and As-built rungs are already there.
3. Full validation, mandatory.
4. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
5. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe); its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
6. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for
   the commits the previous push made permanent; never record a SHA that is not on a permanent
   branch.

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports; getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

67	(`- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, literal `[[N]]` placeholder)

70	close-out; close-out only *finalizes* (title sync, design
71	subsections, retiring the `## In Progress` block). A

73	rung placeholders are backfilled later, once the commit is
74	permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the

at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
for the local-ladder mechanics.

A **chores section** is a `##` section in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
should have a reference to it on a rung of its section's
as-built ladder in a chores file.

The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`).

subsections, retiring the `## In Progress` block). A
single-commit cycle's ladder is one bare-`X.Y.Z` rung. The
rung placeholders are backfilled later, once the commit is
permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

`## Table of Contents`, synced to the final title at
close-out.

design subsection pattern, rung / reference formatting)
live in
[agent-data/notes.md](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions).

An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA, but a SHA
isn't stable until the commit lands on a **permanent

  placeholder**.

[Chores commit references](../agent-data/notes.md#chores-commit-references)).

deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`.
